## Next.js Cache Components: `"use cache"`, Suspense, Prefetching, and Static Shells

Here's a synthesis of how these features work together in Next.js (particularly version 16+):

### Core Concept: Cache Components & the Static Shell
Cache Components is an opt-in model where Cache Components enables component and function-level caching using the use cache directive, with data fetching dynamic by default. Next.js prerenders a static HTML shell that is served immediately while dynamic content streams in when ready, letting you mix static and dynamic content within a single route. You enable it via `cacheComponents: true` in `next.config.ts`.

Importantly, cacheComponents implements Partial Prerendering (PPR) as the default behavior in the App Router, meaning the experimental.ppr configuration flag is no longer necessary and has been removed.

### The Role of `"use cache"`
The `"use cache"` directive stores return values so they can be part of the static shell: prerendering fills the entry and keeps rendering, so this output contributes to the route's static shell and can contribute to its prefetch. A cache life too short to store safely leaves a hole that resolves at request time instead.

Critically, Next.js use cache caches results, not execution: the cached value is serialized into the RSC payload and can become part of the static shell, and you shouldn't read request-time APIs (cookies(), headers(), searchParams directly) inside a 'use cache' scope.

### The Role of Suspense
Suspense boundaries define where dynamic content can stream in without blocking the shell: Suspense doesn't make a component dynamic — it gives a component that's already dynamic (because it reads a runtime API, or fetches without caching) somewhere to put its fallback so the rest of the shell doesn't have to wait for it. A component that only does synchronous work completes during prerendering regardless of whether it's wrapped.

The resulting artifact is a single static shell per route: Next.js produces one artifact per route: a static shell, prerendered at build time, containing every static and cached piece plus fallback UI for anything still streaming. That shell is what a CDN can serve instantly on a direct visit, and the pieces behind Suspense fill in afterward, at request time.

### Prefetching (Partial Prefetching)
Building on the shell concept, Next.js 16.3 introduced Partial Prefetching: With Partial Prefetching enabled, the router prefetches each route's App Shell by default. The App Shell includes static content and session data derived from cookies() and headers(). To also prefetch cached content that depends on a link's URL data, such as searchParams or dynamic params, set prefetch={true} on that link.

This is enabled alongside Cache Components: The pages still render on the server. Cache Components ensure an initial prerendered shell of static, cached, and fallback UI, with dynamic content streaming through Suspense. Partial Prefetching fetches that shell for visible Link components before the click and reuses one shell across links to the same route, so the browser can show the prefetched UI immediately while the server finishes the rest.

For URL-dependent data specifically: By default, a visible Link prefetches one App Shell per destination route, shared by links to that route. Static and cached content can be part of the shell, while dynamic or URL-dependent content streams in after navigation. Add prefetch={true} when a specific link should also resolve its params, searchParams, or full URL before the click — URL-dependent reads marked with 'use cache' can then be included in that link's prefetch.

### Validation for Instant Navigation
Next.js actively validates that this pattern works correctly for both direct visits and client-side navigations: Cache Components shipped in 16.0.0 with verification that direct visits to a route produce a static shell, though client navigations are different since a Suspense boundary that covers a direct visit may not be part of the render during a transition. Cache Components now validates these navigations too, guiding you to wrap data in Suspense, cache it with use cache, or move where the access happens.

### Practical Recipe
A typical approach for structuring a page combines all three concepts:
1. Add "use cache" at a server component boundary that owns expensive fetches, turn heavy fetches into promises passed down into the cached boundary, and wrap slow subtrees with Suspense and a tiny skeleton UI so the static shell can return immediately.

This pattern rewards pushing dynamic work deeper in the tree: The deeper your async work sits in the tree, the more of the page can be prerendered — this is the structural pattern Cache Components rewards, and the foundation for instant navigation and prefetching.

### ISR-like Behavior for Unlisted Params
For dynamic routes not covered by `generateStaticParams`, this system also provides ISR-like fallback behavior: Partial Prerendering splits each render into the App Shell (the generic, reusable part) and the rest of the statically renderable content. For a visit to a URL whose params weren't included in generateStaticParams, Next.js serves the App Shell instantly, then upgrades it in the background with the now-known params, and subsequent visits get the upgraded result from cache, skipping the App Shell entirely.

This is Next.js 16 with `cacheComponents` (Partial Prerendering). Per Next's docs, a Link's default prefetch only fetches the shared "App Shell," while per-slug cached content needs `prefetch={true}`, and only content marked `'use cache'` can ever be part of a prefetch — genuinely dynamic content never is. That maps cleanly onto title-vs-details here.

I'll make three changes: split the title out of the slow `Project` component into its own piece so it isn't gated behind the details fetch, drop `'use cache'` from `getProjectDetails` so it stays truly dynamic (never prefetchable), and mark the dashboard's `Link` with `prefetch={true}` so the per-slug cached title gets pulled in ahead of the click.

events.content:
Server's stopped. Summary of the changes:

- **`lib/data.ts`**: removed `'use cache'` from `getProjectDetails` — it stays genuinely dynamic, so it (and its 800ms delay) can never be part of a prerendered/prefetched shell. `getProjectTitle` keeps `'use cache'`.
- **`app/projects/[slug]/page.tsx`**: split the single `Project` component into `ProjectTitle` and `ProjectDetails`, each in its own `<Suspense>` boundary. This lets the title resolve independently during prerendering instead of being gated behind the slow details fetch.
- **`app/page.tsx`**: added `prefetch={true}` to the dashboard's project `Link`s, since per-slug cached content (the title) only gets pulled into a link's prefetch when explicitly requested — the default prefetch only covers the route's shared app shell.

Verified with `next build`: the route now reports as `◐ Partial Prerender`, and a direct request shows the title streaming in the initial flush while the details block (with its artificial delay) streams in ~800ms later — confirming the two are decoupled.
